## <span class="num">11.4.1</span> Conjugacy Classes in $S_n$

By Theorem [3.4.6](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#theorem-3-4-6), two permutations are conjugate in $S_n$ if and only if they have the same cycle type; the key computation is $$\tau \, (a_1 \, a_2 \, \cdots \, a_k) \, \tau^{-1} = (\tau(a_1) \, \tau(a_2) \, \cdots \, \tau(a_k)).$$ So the conjugacy classes of $S_n$ correspond to the partitions of $n$, and the class equation of $S_n$ is obtained by counting the permutations of each cycle type.

:::example{11.4.1} Conjugacy classes in $S_3$ and $S_4$
For $n = 3$, the partitions $1+1+1$, $2+1$ and $3$ give the identity, the 3 transpositions and the 2 three-cycles: $6 = 1 + 3 + 2$.

For $n = 4$, the five partitions give the identity (1 element), the transpositions ($\binom{4}{2} = 6$), the products $(i\,j)(k\,\ell)$ of two disjoint transpositions (3), the 3-cycles ($4 \cdot 2 = 8$) and the 4-cycles ($3! = 6$). The class equation of $S_4$ is $24 = 1 + 6 + 3 + 8 + 6$.
:::

:::example{11.4.2} Normal subgroups of $S_4$
A normal subgroup of $S_4$ is a union of conjugacy classes containing $\{e\}$, and its order divides 24. Adding 1 to sums of distinct class sizes among $6, 3, 8, 6$, the only divisors of 24 we obtain besides 1 and 24 are $1 + 3 = 4$ and $1 + 3 + 8 = 12$. Both unions are subgroups. The first is $V_4 = \{e, (1\,2)(3\,4), (1\,3)(2\,4), (1\,4)(2\,3)\}$, the ***Klein four-group***: each non-identity element has order 2, and the product of two distinct ones is the third (for instance $(1\,2)(3\,4) \cdot (1\,3)(2\,4) = (1\,4)(2\,3)$), so $V_4 \cong \ZZ/2 \times \ZZ/2$. The second consists of the identity, the elements $(i\,j)(k\,\ell)$ and the 3-cycles, which are exactly the even permutations; it is $A_4$. So the normal subgroups of $S_4$ are $\{e\}$, $V_4$, $A_4$ and $S_4$.
:::

## <span class="num">11.4.2</span> Conjugacy Classes in $A_n$

Recall the sign homomorphism $\sgn : S_n \to \{\pm 1\}$ (Definition [3.4.10](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#definition-3-4-10)) and the alternating group $A_n = \ker(\sgn)$ (Definition [3.4.15](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#definition-3-4-15)), a normal subgroup of index 2 in $S_n$ for $n \geq 2$. Transpositions are odd, and a $k$-cycle is a product of $k - 1$ transpositions, $(i_1 \, i_2 \, \cdots \, i_k) = (i_1 \, i_2)(i_2 \, i_3) \cdots (i_{k-1} \, i_k)$, so it has sign $(-1)^{k-1}$. Hence $\sigma \in A_n$ if and only if its cycle decomposition has an even number of cycles of even length.

A conjugacy class of $S_n$ contained in $A_n$ is a union of conjugacy classes of $A_n$, but it need not be a single class: conjugating by elements of $A_n$ only, we may reach fewer elements.

:::proposition{11.4.3} Splitting of conjugacy classes in $A_n$
Let $C$ be a conjugacy class of $S_n$, $n \geq 2$. Then either $C \cap A_n = \emptyset$ or $C \subseteq A_n$. In the second case, let $\sigma \in C$. Then exactly one of the following holds.

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. Some odd permutation commutes with $\sigma$, that is, $Z_{S_n}(\sigma) \not\subseteq A_n$; then $C$ is a single conjugacy class of $A_n$.
2. $Z_{S_n}(\sigma) \subseteq A_n$; then $C$ splits into two conjugacy classes of $A_n$, each with $|C|/2$ elements.
:::

:::proof
Since $A_n$ is normal, it contains the $S_n$-conjugacy class of each of its elements; so if $C$ meets $A_n$, then $C \subseteq A_n$. Suppose $C \subseteq A_n$, and fix an odd permutation $\tau$. Then $S_n = A_n \sqcup A_n\tau$, so $$C = \{h\sigma h^{-1} : h \in A_n\} \cup \{(h\tau)\sigma(h\tau)^{-1} : h \in A_n\} = C' \cup C'',$$ where $C'$ is the $A_n$-conjugacy class of $\sigma$ and $C''$ is the $A_n$-conjugacy class of $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$. Two conjugacy classes of $A_n$ are equal or disjoint, and $C' = C''$ if and only if $\sigma \in C''$, that is, $\sigma = g\sigma g^{-1}$ for some $g = h\tau$ with $h \in A_n$. The elements $h\tau$ are exactly the odd permutations, so $C' = C''$ if and only if some odd permutation commutes with $\sigma$. In case (b), conjugation by $\tau$ maps $C'$ into $C''$ (it sends $h\sigma h^{-1}$ to $(\tau h \tau^{-1})(\tau\sigma\tau^{-1})(\tau h\tau^{-1})^{-1}$, and $\tau h \tau^{-1} \in A_n$), and conjugation by $\tau^{-1}$ maps $C''$ into $C'$ in the same way. These maps are inverse to each other, so $|C'| = |C''| = |C|/2$.
:::

:::proposition{11.4.4} When a class splits
Let $\sigma \in A_n$, and count the fixed points of $\sigma$ as cycles of length 1. The $S_n$-conjugacy class of $\sigma$ splits into two conjugacy classes of $A_n$ if and only if the cycle lengths of $\sigma$ are all odd and pairwise distinct. (In particular, if it splits, $\sigma$ has at most one fixed point.)
:::

:::proof
Suppose first that $\sigma$ has a cycle $c$ of even length. Then $c$ commutes with $\sigma$ (it commutes with itself and with the other cycles of $\sigma$, which are disjoint from it), and $c$ is odd. Suppose next that $\sigma$ has two cycles $(a_1 \, \cdots \, a_k)$ and $(b_1 \, \cdots \, b_k)$ of the same odd length $k$; for $k = 1$ these are two fixed points $a_1$ and $b_1$. Then $\tau = (a_1 \, b_1)(a_2 \, b_2) \cdots (a_k \, b_k)$ is a product of $k$ disjoint transpositions, hence odd, and by the key computation $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1} = \sigma$: conjugation by $\tau$ exchanges the two cycles and fixes the other cycles of $\sigma$, whose entries $\tau$ does not move. In both cases $Z_{S_n}(\sigma) \not\subseteq A_n$, and the class does not split by Proposition [11.4.3](/notes/math-55a/11-4-conjugacy-in-s-n-and-a-n#proposition-11-4-3).

Conversely, suppose the cycle lengths of $\sigma$ are odd and pairwise distinct, let $X_1, \ldots, X_\ell$ be the supports of the cycles $c_1, \ldots, c_\ell$ of $\sigma$ (including the 1-cycles), and let $\tau$ commute with $\sigma$. By the key computation, the cycles of $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1} = \sigma$ are obtained by applying $\tau$ to the entries of the cycles of $\sigma$; by the uniqueness of the cycle decomposition (Theorem [3.4.1](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#theorem-3-4-1)), $\tau$ maps each $X_j$ onto the support of a cycle of $\sigma$ of the same length, which is $X_j$ itself because the lengths are distinct. Write $c_j = (a_1 \, a_2 \, \cdots \, a_k)$. Then $(\tau(a_1) \, \tau(a_2) \, \cdots \, \tau(a_k)) = c_j$, so $\tau(a_{i+1}) = c_j(\tau(a_i))$ for each $i$; if $\tau(a_1) = c_j^m(a_1)$, it follows that $\tau(a_i) = c_j^{i-1}(\tau(a_1)) = c_j^m(a_i)$ for all $i$. So $\tau$ agrees with $c_j^{m_j}$ on $X_j$ for some $m_j$, and $\tau = c_1^{m_1} \cdots c_\ell^{m_\ell}$. Each $c_j$ is a cycle of odd length, hence even, so $\tau$ is even. Thus $Z_{S_n}(\sigma) \subseteq A_n$, and the class splits by Proposition [11.4.3](/notes/math-55a/11-4-conjugacy-in-s-n-and-a-n#proposition-11-4-3).
:::

:::example{11.4.5} Conjugacy classes of $A_4$ and $A_5$
In $A_4$, the three elements $(i\,j)(k\,\ell)$ form one class (they have cycles of even length), while the eight 3-cycles, with cycle lengths $3, 1$, split into two classes of 4; for instance $(1\,2\,3)$ and $(1\,3\,2) = (2\,3)(1\,2\,3)(2\,3)^{-1}$ are not conjugate in $A_4$. The class equation of $A_4$ is $12 = 1 + 3 + 4 + 4$. The Klein four-group $V_4$ is normal in $S_4$, hence in $A_4$; so $A_4$ is not simple.

In $A_5$, the 15 elements $(i\,j)(k\,\ell)$ form one class (for instance, the odd permutation $(1\,2)$ commutes with $(1\,2)(3\,4)$), and so do the 20 three-cycles, with cycle lengths $3, 1, 1$ (for instance, $(4\,5)$ commutes with $(1\,2\,3)$). The 24 five-cycles split into two classes of 12. The class equation of $A_5$ is $$60 = 1 + 15 + 20 + 12 + 12.$$
:::

:::corollary{11.4.6} 3-cycles are conjugate in $A_n$
For $n \geq 5$, the 3-cycles form a single conjugacy class of $A_n$.
:::

:::proof
The 3-cycles form a conjugacy class of $S_n$, contained in $A_n$. A 3-cycle has $n - 3 \geq 2$ fixed points, that is, two cycles of length 1, so by Proposition [11.4.4](/notes/math-55a/11-4-conjugacy-in-s-n-and-a-n#proposition-11-4-4) this class does not split.
:::

For $n = 4$ the corollary fails, as the example shows; this is where the hypothesis $n \geq 5$ of the next theorem enters.

## <span class="num">11.4.3</span> Simplicity of $A_n$

Recall that a group is *simple* if its only normal subgroups are $\{e\}$ and the group itself.

:::theorem{11.4.7} Simplicity of $A_5$
The alternating group $A_5$ is simple.
:::

:::proof
A normal subgroup $H$ of $A_5$ is a union of conjugacy classes of $A_5$ containing $\{e\}$, and $|H|$ divides 60. By Example [11.4.5](/notes/math-55a/11-4-conjugacy-in-s-n-and-a-n#example-11-4-5), $|H| = 1 + s$, where $s$ is a sum of distinct terms of the list $15, 20, 12, 12$. The possible values of $1 + s$ are $1, 13, 16, 21, 25, 28, 33, 36, 40, 45, 48, 60$, and of these only 1 and 60 divide 60. So $H = \{e\}$ or $H = A_5$.
:::

For larger $n$ we argue with 3-cycles.

:::lemma{11.4.8} $A_n$ is generated by 3-cycles
For $n \geq 3$, every element of $A_n$ is a product of 3-cycles.
:::

:::proof
By induction on $n$. For $n = 3$, $A_3 = \{e, (1\,2\,3), (1\,3\,2)\}$ and the claim is clear. Let $n \geq 4$, assume the claim for $A_{n-1}$, and let $\sigma \in A_n$. If $\sigma(n) = n$, then $\sigma$ is an even permutation of $\{1, \ldots, n-1\}$, so it is a product of 3-cycles by induction. Otherwise, let $i = \sigma(n) \neq n$ and let $j$ be any element distinct from $i$ and $n$. The 3-cycle $(j \, i \, n)$ sends $i$ to $n$, so $\tau = (j \, i \, n)\sigma \in A_n$ satisfies $\tau(n) = n$, and $\tau$ is a product of 3-cycles by the first case. Hence so is $\sigma = (j \, i \, n)^{-1}\tau = (n \, i \, j)\tau$.
:::

:::theorem{11.4.9} Simplicity of $A_n$
For every $n \geq 5$, the alternating group $A_n$ is simple.
:::

:::proof
Let $H$ be a normal subgroup of $A_n$ with $H \neq \{e\}$. If $H$ contains a 3-cycle, it contains all 3-cycles, since they form one conjugacy class of $A_n$ (Corollary [11.4.6](/notes/math-55a/11-4-conjugacy-in-s-n-and-a-n#corollary-11-4-6)); then $H = A_n$ by Lemma [11.4.8](/notes/math-55a/11-4-conjugacy-in-s-n-and-a-n#lemma-11-4-8). So it suffices to find a 3-cycle in $H$. Throughout, we use that for $\sigma \in H$ and $g \in A_n$, the element $g\sigma g^{-1}\sigma^{-1}$ lies in $H$, because $g\sigma g^{-1} \in H$. Products are composed from right to left.

Choose $\sigma \in H$, $\sigma \neq e$. If $\sigma$ has order $m$ and $p$ is a prime dividing $m$, then $\sigma^{m/p} \in H$ has order $p$; so we may assume that $\sigma$ has prime order $p$. Its disjoint cycles $c_1, \ldots, c_\ell$ commute, so $e = \sigma^p = c_1^p \cdots c_\ell^p$; the $c_i^p$ move disjoint sets of points, so each $c_i^p = e$. A $k$-cycle has order $k$, so every cycle of $\sigma$ of length greater than 1 has length $p$: $\sigma$ is a product of disjoint $p$-cycles.

**Case 1: $p \geq 5$.** Write $\sigma = (i_1 \, i_2 \, i_3 \, i_4 \, i_5 \, \cdots \, i_p)\tau$, where $\tau$ is the product of the other $p$-cycles of $\sigma$ and fixes $i_1, \ldots, i_p$. Let $g = (i_4 \, i_3 \, i_2)$, so $g^{-1} = (i_2 \, i_3 \, i_4)$. Applying $\sigma^{-1}$, $g^{-1}$, $\sigma$, $g$ in turn, $$\begin{array}{r@{\;\mapsto\;}c@{\;\mapsto\;}c@{\;\mapsto\;}c@{\;\mapsto\;}l}
i_1 & i_p & i_p & i_1 & i_1, \\
i_2 & i_1 & i_1 & i_2 & i_4, \\
i_3 & i_2 & i_3 & i_4 & i_3, \\
i_4 & i_3 & i_4 & i_5 & i_5, \\
i_5 & i_4 & i_2 & i_3 & i_2.
\end{array}$$ Any other point $x$ is fixed: neither $x$ nor $\sigma^{-1}(x)$ lies in $\{i_2, i_3, i_4\}$, so $g^{-1}$ and $g$ do not move them. Hence $$g\sigma g^{-1}\sigma^{-1} = (i_2 \, i_4 \, i_5) \in H.$$

**Case 2: $p = 3$.** If $\sigma$ is a 3-cycle we are done. Otherwise $\sigma = (i_1 \, i_2 \, i_3)(i_4 \, i_5 \, i_6)\tau$, with $\tau$ fixing $i_1, \ldots, i_6$. With $g = (i_4 \, i_3 \, i_2)$, the same kind of computation gives $g\sigma g^{-1}\sigma^{-1} = (i_1 \, i_5 \, i_2 \, i_4 \, i_3)$, an element of $H$ of order 5, and Case 1 applies to it.

**Case 3: $p = 2$, and $\sigma$ is a product of two transpositions,** $\sigma = (i_1 \, i_2)(i_3 \, i_4)$. Since $n \geq 5$, there is a point $i_5 \notin \{i_1, i_2, i_3, i_4\}$. With $g = (i_5 \, i_3 \, i_1)$, we get $g\sigma g^{-1}\sigma^{-1} = (i_1 \, i_5 \, i_2 \, i_4 \, i_3)$, of order 5, and Case 1 applies.

**Case 4: $p = 2$, and $\sigma$ is a product of more than two transpositions.** Since $\sigma$ is even, it has at least four, and $\sigma = (i_1 \, i_2)(i_3 \, i_4)(i_5 \, i_6)\tau$ with $\tau$ fixing $i_1, \ldots, i_6$. With $g = (i_5 \, i_3 \, i_1)$, we get $g\sigma g^{-1}\sigma^{-1} = (i_1 \, i_5 \, i_3)(i_2 \, i_4 \, i_6)$, an element of $H$ of order 3, and Case 2 applies.
:::

:::corollary{11.4.10} Normal subgroups of $S_n$
For $n \geq 5$, the only normal subgroups of $S_n$ are $\{e\}$, $A_n$ and $S_n$.
:::

:::proof
Let $H \trianglelefteq S_n$. Then $H \cap A_n$ is normal in $S_n$, hence in $A_n$, so $H \cap A_n$ is $\{e\}$ or $A_n$ by Theorem [11.4.9](/notes/math-55a/11-4-conjugacy-in-s-n-and-a-n#theorem-11-4-9). If $A_n \subseteq H$, then $H = A_n$ or $H = S_n$, since $A_n$ has index 2. If $H \cap A_n = \{e\}$, then $H$ contains at most one odd permutation (if $h_1, h_2 \in H$ are odd, then $h_1^{-1}h_2 \in H \cap A_n$, so $h_1 = h_2$), and $|H| \leq 2$. Suppose $H = \{e, \sigma\}$ with $\sigma \neq e$. Since $H$ is normal, $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1} = \sigma$ for every $\tau \in S_n$. But $\sigma$ has a cycle $(a_1 \, a_2 \, \cdots)$ of length at least 2, and as $n \geq 3$ there is a point $b \notin \{a_1, a_2\}$; for $\tau = (a_2 \, b)$, $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}(a_1) = \tau(\sigma(a_1)) = \tau(a_2) = b \neq \sigma(a_1)$, a contradiction. So $H = \{e\}$.
:::
